description: I’m Ian—a drummer, gamer, coder, and explorer of the unknown. I’m fascinated by astrophysics, planets, moons, space exploration, and the transformative potential of AI. Drumming has taught me precision and discipline; coding fuels my problem-solving; and presenting lets me turn complex ideas into compelling stories. I don’t just look at the stars—I wonder what’s waiting beyond them.
summary:
Still Out There: Meet NASA’s Space Machines! 

Did you know that some of NASA’s space machines are still out there, even after their missions have ended? They may never return to Earth, but their discoveries continue to inspire us! 
Still Out There is a fun, free, and interactive learning app for children aged 8–13. It introduces 25 real NASA machines, including landers, rovers, mirrors and space probes, left on the Moon, Mars or travelling through deep space. 
Children can spin a 3D globe of the Moon or Mars, explore the Solar System, and discover where each machine is located. Tap on a machine and hear it tell its own story! Learn how it worked, what it discovered, and how it helped us understand space. 
The app also offers six narrators to read stories aloud, with words highlighted as they play. Children can even follow Voyager 1’s journey towards reaching one light day from Earth! 
Why is it special? 
Still Out There makes space exploration exciting and easy to understand. It sparks curiosity about science, technology, and engineering, showing children that discoveries continue long after a mission ends. 
Best of all, it is completely free, needs no sign-in, works offline, and is designed to be accessible to young learners. 
Explore the universe, meet its forgotten explorers, and discover the machines that are still out there!
details:
Still Out There

What it does: Still Out There is a free web app for kids aged 8 - 13 that introduces 25 NASA machines still on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Kids spin a Moon or Mars globe, or open a Solar System map, then tap a machine at its real landing site. Each machine tells its own story in the first person: how it worked, what we learned, and where it is now. "Read to me" reads the story aloud in a choice of six narrator voices and highlights each paragraph as it goes. There's also a live Voyager 1 distance counter, a timeline and a quiz.

Benefits and impact: It turns space hardware into characters kids remember, and shows that exploration doesn't end at launch. It's free, needs no sign-in, works on phones, installs like an app and works offline. It's accessible too: read-aloud, a font designed for low-vision readers, keyboard support and reduced motion. A notes section for teachers and grown-ups explains who it's for and where the facts come from.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Canvas and SVG for the globes and map; offline support so it installs like an app; Apple's Mac text-to-speech voices for the narration; Netlify hosting; and facts from NASA mission pages, NASA's NSSDCA archive and the Lunar and Planetary Institute. Claude (an AI from Anthropic) helped write the code, stories and slides, and this is labelled in the app.

Creativity: The machines narrate their own lives inside a mission-control-style interface, and a log-scale map fits Earth and Voyager 1 on one screen.

What we considered: Reading level, accuracy, accessibility, offline use, and no NASA logos, flags or mission patches.
